title: Chapter 16 — The Ship
paragraphs: That night in bed, we made our plans for the next day. But to my surprise and real concern, Queequeg informed me that he had been consulting Yojo — the name of his small black idol — and Yojo had told him two or three times over, insisting on the point, that instead of going together to the harbor to pick out a whaling ship, the choice should rest entirely with me. Yojo intended to help us, and had already selected a vessel. If left to myself, I, Ishmael, would find it as if by chance. I was to sign on immediately, without waiting for Queequeg.

I should mention that Queequeg placed great trust in Yojo's judgment and remarkable ability to predict things. He regarded Yojo with considerable respect, as a fairly decent sort of god who probably meant well overall, but who didn't always succeed in his well-meaning plans.

Now, this plan of Queequeg's — or rather Yojo's — about choosing our ship, I didn't like it one bit. I had been counting on Queequeg's good judgment to point out the whaler best suited to carry us safely. But since all my objections had no effect on him, I had to give in. So I prepared to tackle the business with a determined burst of energy that should quickly settle the matter. Early the next morning, I left Queequeg shut up with Yojo in our little bedroom — it seemed to be some sort of Lent or Ramadan, a day of fasting, self-denial, and prayer for Queequeg and Yojo. How it all worked, I could never figure out, since I never managed to master his rituals and articles of faith. So, leaving Queequeg fasting with his tomahawk pipe, and Yojo warming himself by his little sacrificial fire of wood shavings, I headed out among the ships. After much wandering and many random questions, I learned there were three ships preparing for three-year voyages: The Devil-Dam, the Tit-Bit, and the Pequod. Devil-Dam — I have no idea where the name came from. Tit-Bit is obvious. Pequod, you'll probably remember, was the name of a famous Massachusetts Indian tribe, now extinct as the ancient Medes. I looked over the Devil-Dam, hopped across to the Tit-Bit, and finally, going aboard the Pequod and looking around for a moment, I decided this was the ship for us.

You may have seen plenty of strange vessels in your time, for all I know — square-toed luggers, towering Japanese junks, boxy galliots, and who knows what else. But take my word for it, you never saw such a rare old ship as this Pequod. She was old school, on the small side if anything, with an old-fashioned, claw-footed look about her. Seasoned and weather-stained through the typhoons and calms of all four oceans, her old hull had darkened like a French soldier who has fought in both Egypt and Siberia. Her sturdy bow looked bearded with age. Her masts — cut somewhere on the coast of Japan, after she lost the originals overboard in a gale — stood stiffly upright like the spines of three old Cologne kings. Her ancient decks were worn and wrinkled, like the pilgrim-worshipped flagstone in Canterbury Cathedral where Becket bled. But on top of all these antiquities, she had new and marvelous features related to the wild business she had followed for more than half a century. Old Captain Peleg, who served many years as her chief mate before commanding his own vessel and was now retired and one of the Pequod's principal owners — this old Peleg, during his time as chief mate, had built upon the ship's original strangeness and decorated it all over with a uniqueness of material and design matched by nothing except perhaps a Viking's carved shield or bedstead. She was decked out like some barbarian African emperor, his neck heavy with polished ivory pendants. She was a thing of trophies. A cannibal of a craft, adorning herself with the carved bones of her enemies. All around, her open bulwarks were lined like one continuous jaw, set with the long sharp teeth of sperm whales, used as pins to fasten her old ropes and rigging. Those ropes didn't run through ordinary wooden blocks but traveled smoothly over sheaves of sea-ivory. Scorning a standard wheel at her noble helm, she carried instead a tiller — and that tiller was carved in one mass from the long narrow lower jaw of her hereditary enemy. The helmsman steering by that tiller in a storm felt like a Tartar holding back his wild horse by gripping its jaw. A noble craft, but somehow deeply melancholy. All noble things carry that touch.

When I looked around the quarter-deck for someone in authority, wanting to offer myself for the voyage, at first I saw nobody. But I couldn't miss a strange sort of tent, or rather wigwam, set up a little behind the mainmast. It seemed to be a temporary structure used only in port. It was cone-shaped, about ten feet high, made from the long, huge slabs of flexible black bone taken from the middle and highest part of a right whale's jaw. Planted with their broad ends on the deck, a circle of these slabs leaned inward toward each other, joined at the top in a tufted point where loose hairy fibers waved back and forth like the topknot on some old Native chief's head. A triangular opening faced the bow of the ship, giving whoever sat inside a clear view forward.

Half hidden in this strange shelter, I finally found someone who looked like he had authority. It was noon, the ship's work was paused, and he was enjoying a break from the burden of command. He sat in an old-fashioned oak chair, elaborately carved all over, its seat woven from the same springy material as the wigwam.

There was nothing especially remarkable about the elderly man I saw. He was brown and muscular, like most old seamen, and heavily bundled in blue pilot-cloth cut in the Quaker style. The only notable thing was a fine, almost microscopic network of the tiniest wrinkles around his eyes, which must have come from years of sailing through hard gales and always squinting into the wind — that habit tightens the muscles around the eyes. Wrinkles like that are very effective in a scowl.
"Is this the Captain of the Pequod?" I said, stepping up to the entrance of the tent.
"Supposing it is the captain of the Pequod, what do you want with him?" he demanded.
"I was thinking of signing on."
"Were you now? I can see you're no Nantucketer. Ever been in a stove boat?"
"No, Sir, I never have."
"Don't know anything at all about whaling, I suppose — eh?"
"Nothing, Sir, but I have no doubt I'll learn quickly. I've made several voyages in the merchant service, and I think that —"

"Merchant service be damned. Don't talk that language to me. See this leg? I'll take that leg off your stern if you ever mention the merchant service to me again. Merchant service indeed! I suppose you feel quite proud of having served on those merchant ships. But flukes! Man, what makes you want to go whaling, eh? Looks a little suspicious, doesn't it? Haven't been a pirate, have you? Didn't rob your last captain, did you? Aren't planning to murder the officers once you're at sea?"

I protested my innocence. I could see that behind these half-humorous accusations, this old seaman, as a sheltered Quaker Nantucketer, was full of his island prejudices. He was suspicious of all outsiders unless they came from Cape Cod or the Vineyard.
"But what draws you to whaling? I want to know that before I think about signing you on."
"Well, sir, I want to see what whaling is. I want to see the world."
"Want to see what whaling is, eh? Have you set eyes on Captain Ahab?"
"Who is Captain Ahab, sir?"
"That's what I thought. Captain Ahab is the captain of this ship."
"I'm mistaken then. I thought I was speaking to the captain himself."

"You're speaking to Captain Peleg — that's who you're speaking to, young man. It's my job, mine and Captain Bildad's, to see the Pequod fitted out for the voyage and supplied with everything she needs, including crew. We're part owners and agents. But as I was saying, if you want to know what whaling is, as you say you do, I can show you a way to find out before you commit yourself past backing out. Take a look at Captain Ahab, young man, and you'll find he has only one leg."
"What do you mean, sir? Was the other one lost to a whale?"
"Lost to a whale! Young man, come closer: it was devoured, chewed up, crunched by the most monstrous sperm whale that ever smashed a boat! — ah, ah!"

I was a little alarmed by his intensity, and perhaps also a little moved by the genuine grief in that final exclamation. But I said as calmly as I could, "What you say is no doubt true enough, sir. But how could I have known there was anything especially ferocious about that particular whale, though I might have guessed as much from the simple fact of the accident."
"Look here, young man, you're a bit soft, do you see? You don't talk tough at all. You have been to sea before, surely?"
"Sir," said I, "I thought I told you that I'd been on four voyages in the merchant —"

"Stop right there! Remember what I said about the merchant service — don't push me — I won't have it. But let's understand each other. I've given you a hint about what whaling involves. Do you still feel inclined to try it?"
"I do, sir."
"Very good. Now, are you the kind of man who'd throw a harpoon down a live whale's throat and then jump in after it? Answer quick!"
"I am, sir, if it were absolutely necessary and there were no alternative — which I don't believe is actually the case."

"Good again. So you not only want to go whaling to find out what it's like, but you also want to see the world? Wasn't that what you said? I thought so. Well then, just step forward there and take a look over the weather bow. Then come back and tell me what you see."

For a moment I stood puzzled by this odd request, not sure whether to take it as a joke or seriously. But when Captain Peleg concentrated all his crow's feet into one fierce scowl, he sent me on my way.

Walking forward and looking over the weather bow, I saw that the ship, swinging on her anchor with the rising tide, was now pointing toward the open ocean. The view was unlimited but utterly monotonous and forbidding. Not the slightest variety that I could see.
"Well, what's the report?" said Peleg when I came back. "What did you see?"
"Not much," I replied. "Nothing but water. Plenty of horizon, though, and there's a squall coming up, I think."
"Well, what do you think now about seeing the world? Still want to go around Cape Horn to see more of it, eh? Can't you see the world right where you stand?"

I was a little taken aback, but go whaling I must and would. The Pequod was as good a ship as any — I thought the best — and I repeated all this to Peleg. Seeing how determined I was, he agreed to sign me on.
"You might as well sign the papers right now," he added. "Come along." And with that, he led the way below deck into the cabin.

Sitting on the stern bench was what struck me as a most unusual and surprising figure. This turned out to be Captain Bildad, who along with Captain Peleg was one of the largest owners of the vessel. The remaining shares, as is sometimes the case in these ports, were held by a crowd of old pensioners — widows, orphaned children, and wards of the court — each owning about the value of a timber head, a foot of plank, or a nail or two in the ship. People in Nantucket invest their money in whaling vessels the same way you invest yours in government bonds.

Now, Bildad, like Peleg and indeed many Nantucketers, was a Quaker. The island had originally been settled by that sect, and to this day its inhabitants generally retain Quaker peculiarities to an unusual degree, though strangely modified by completely foreign influences. Some of these Quakers are the most bloodthirsty of all sailors and whale hunters. They are fighting Quakers — Quakers with a vengeance.

Among them you find men who were given Scripture names — a remarkably common custom on the island — and who grew up naturally absorbing the stately "thee" and "thou" of Quaker speech. Yet from the bold, daring, boundless adventure of their later lives, they strangely blend these inherited mannerisms with a thousand dashing traits worthy of a Scandinavian sea-king or a heroic pagan Roman. And when these qualities come together in a man of greatly superior natural force, with a powerful mind and a deep heart — a man who, through the stillness and solitude of many long night watches in remote waters, under constellations never seen in the north, has been led to think independently and unconventionally, taking in all of nature's sweet or savage impressions straight from her own wild breast, and thereby learning a bold, forceful, elevated way of speaking — that man is one in a million, a mighty figure shaped for noble tragedies. It won't detract from him, dramatically speaking, if by birth or circumstance he carries what seems a half-willful, overriding darkness at the bottom of his nature. For all tragically great men are made so through a certain darkness. Be sure of this, young ambition: all mortal greatness is but disease. But we're not dealing with such a man yet — rather with quite another, and still a man whose peculiarities stem from yet another strain of the Quaker character, shaped by individual circumstances.

Like Captain Peleg, Captain Bildad was a well-off, retired whaleman. But unlike Peleg — who didn't give a damn about what people call serious things and considered those very serious things the biggest trifles of all — Captain Bildad had been raised in the strictest Nantucket Quaker tradition. And all his years at sea, all the sights of lovely unclothed island women round the Horn — none of it had moved this born Quaker one inch or changed a single angle of his vest. Yet for all this unchangeableness, there was something inconsistent about worthy Captain Bildad. Though his conscience wouldn't allow him to bear arms against invaders on land, he had boundlessly invaded the Atlantic and Pacific. Though a sworn enemy of human bloodshed, he had, in his strait-laced coat, spilled barrels upon barrels of whale blood. How, in the reflective evening of his days, the pious Bildad reconciled these things in his memory, I don't know. But it didn't seem to bother him much. Very likely he had long since reached the wise and practical conclusion that a man's religion is one thing and the real world quite another. This world pays dividends. Rising from a little cabin boy in drab short pants to a harpooner in a wide-bellied waistcoat, then boat-header, chief mate, captain, and finally ship owner, Bildad, as I mentioned, had capped off his adventurous career by retiring completely from active life at the respectable age of sixty. He dedicated his remaining days to the quiet collection of his well-earned income.

Now, Bildad, I'm sorry to say, had the reputation of being a hopeless old miser, and in his sea-going days, a bitter, hard taskmaster. They told me in Nantucket, though it certainly seems a curious story, that when he sailed the old Categut whaler, his crew, upon arriving home, were mostly all carried ashore to the hospital, utterly exhausted and worn out. For a pious man, especially a Quaker, he was certainly rather hard-hearted, to say the least. He never swore at his men, they said. But somehow he got an enormous amount of cruel, unrelenting hard work out of them. When Bildad was chief mate, having his drab-colored eye fixed intently on you made you feel completely nervous until you could grab something — a hammer or a marlinspike — and go to work like a madman at something or other, never mind what. Laziness and idleness withered before him. His own body was the perfect expression of his utilitarian character. On his long, gaunt frame, he carried no spare flesh and no unnecessary beard — just a soft, economical fuzz on his chin, like the worn nap of his broad-brimmed hat.

Such was the person I saw sitting on the stern bench when I followed Captain Peleg down into the cabin. The space between the decks was small. There, bolt upright, sat old Bildad, who always sat that way and never leaned — this to preserve his coat tails. His broad-brimmed hat was placed beside him. His legs were stiffly crossed. His drab vest was buttoned up to his chin. And with spectacles on his nose, he seemed absorbed in reading from a heavy volume.
"Bildad," cried Captain Peleg, "at it again, Bildad, eh? You've been studying those Scriptures now for the last thirty years, to my certain knowledge. How far have you got, Bildad?"
As if long accustomed to such irreverent talk from his old shipmate, Bildad paid no attention to the disrespect. He quietly looked up, saw me, and glanced inquiringly at Peleg.
"He says he's our man, Bildad," said Peleg. "He wants to sign on."
"Does thee?" said Bildad, in a hollow tone, turning to face me.
"I does," I said, unconsciously mimicking him — he was that intense a Quaker.
"What do you think of him, Bildad?" said Peleg.
"He'll do," said Bildad, looking me over. Then he went back to reading from his book in a mumbling tone, quite audible.

I thought him the strangest old Quaker I'd ever seen, especially since Peleg, his friend and old shipmate, seemed like such a blowhard. But I said nothing, only looking around me sharply. Peleg threw open a chest, pulled out the ship's articles, set pen and ink before him, and sat down at a small table. I began to think it was time to figure out what terms I'd accept for the voyage. I already knew that in the whaling business they paid no wages. Instead, everyone, including the captain, received shares of the profits called lays. These lays were proportional to the importance of each man's duties. I also knew that as a greenhand at whaling, my own lay wouldn't be large. But considering that I was used to the sea, could steer a ship and splice a rope, I felt confident I'd be offered at least the 275th lay — that is, the 275th part of the voyage's net profits, whatever that might amount to. And though the 275th lay was what they called a rather long lay, it was better than nothing. If we had a lucky voyage, it might nearly cover the cost of the clothes I'd wear out, to say nothing of three years' food and board, for which I wouldn't have to pay a penny.

You might think this was a poor way to build a fortune — and so it was, a very poor way indeed. But I'm one of those people who never fuss about fortunes. I'm quite content if the world is ready to feed and house me while I'm staying at this grim sign of the Thunder Cloud. All things considered, the 275th lay seemed about fair, though I wouldn't have been surprised to be offered the 200th, given my broad shoulders.

But one thing made me uneasy about getting a generous share of the profits. Ashore, I had heard about both Captain Peleg and his strange old crony Bildad — how, being the principal owners of the Pequod, the other smaller shareholders left nearly all management of the ship's business to these two. I suspected that stingy old Bildad might have a lot of say in hiring the crew, especially since I now found him aboard the Pequod, completely at home in the cabin, reading his Bible as if by his own fireside. While Peleg was struggling to sharpen a pen with his jackknife, old Bildad — to my considerable surprise, given that he was such an interested party in these proceedings — paid us no attention at all. He just went on mumbling to himself from his book: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth —"
"Well, Captain Bildad," Peleg interrupted, "what do you say? What lay shall we give this young man?"
"Thou knowest best," came the sepulchral reply. "The seven hundred and seventy-seventh wouldn't be too much, would it? — 'where moth and rust do corrupt, but lay —'"

Lay indeed, I thought, and what a lay! The seven hundred and seventy-seventh! Well, old Bildad, you're determined that I, for one, won't be laying up many lays down here where moth and rust corrupt. It was an absurdly long lay. Though the number sounds impressive to a landlubber, the slightest thought will show you that the seven hundred and seventy-seventh part of a farthing is a great deal less than seven hundred and seventy-seven gold doubloons. And so I thought at the time.
"Why, blast your eyes, Bildad," cried Peleg, "you don't want to swindle this young man! He must have more than that."
"Seven hundred and seventy-seventh," Bildad said again, without lifting his eyes. Then he went on mumbling: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."
"I'm putting him down for the three hundredth," said Peleg. "Do you hear that, Bildad? The three hundredth lay, I say."

Bildad laid down his book and, turning solemnly toward Peleg, said, "Captain Peleg, thou hast a generous heart. But thou must consider thy duty to the other owners of this ship — widows and orphans, many of them — and that if we reward this young man too generously, we may be taking bread from those widows and orphans. The seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay, Captain Peleg."

"Bildad!" roared Peleg, jumping up and stomping around the cabin. "Blast you, Captain Bildad, if I had followed your advice in these matters, I would by now have a conscience heavy enough to sink the largest ship that ever sailed around Cape Horn."

"Captain Peleg," said Bildad steadily, "thy conscience may draw ten inches of water, or ten fathoms — I can't tell. But since thou art still an unrepentant man, Captain Peleg, I greatly fear thy conscience is a leaky one. In the end it will sink thee down to the fiery pit, Captain Peleg."

"Fiery pit! Fiery pit! You insult me, man — beyond all natural bearing, you insult me. It's an outrage to tell any human being he's bound for hell. Flukes and flames! Bildad, say that to me again, and I'll — I'll — yes, I'll swallow a live goat with all his hair and horns on. Out of the cabin, you droning, drab-colored son of a wooden gun — straight out with you!"
As he thundered this out, he rushed at Bildad. But with a marvelous sideways, sliding quickness, Bildad dodged him.

Alarmed by this terrible outburst between the two principal owners of the ship, and half thinking of giving up the whole idea of sailing on a vessel so questionably owned and temporarily commanded, I stepped aside from the door to let Bildad escape. Surely he'd want to flee from Peleg's wrath. But to my astonishment, he sat back down on the bench very quietly and showed not the slightest intention of leaving. He seemed completely used to Peleg and his ways. As for Peleg, after blowing off his rage, he seemed to have no more left in him. He too sat down like a lamb, though he still twitched a little with nervous agitation. "Whew!" he finally whistled. "The squall's blown off to leeward, I think. Bildad, you used to be good at sharpening a lance — sharpen that pen for me, will you? My jackknife needs a grindstone. That's it — thank you, Bildad. Now then, young man, Ishmael's your name, didn't you say? Well then, down you go here, Ishmael, for the three hundredth lay."
"Captain Peleg," said I, "I have a friend who wants to sign on too — shall I bring him down tomorrow?"
"Of course," said Peleg. "Bring him along and we'll have a look at him."
"What lay does he want?" groaned Bildad, glancing up from the book in which he had again buried himself.
"Oh, never mind about that, Bildad," said Peleg. "Has he ever whaled?" turning to me.
"Killed more whales than I can count, Captain Peleg."
"Well, bring him along then."
And after signing the papers, off I went, fully confident that I had done a good morning's work and that the Pequod was the very ship Yojo had chosen to carry Queequeg and me around the Cape.

But I hadn't gone far before it struck me that the captain I was to sail with still remained unseen. In many cases, a whale ship will be completely fitted out and take on her entire crew before the captain shows up to take command. Sometimes these voyages last so long, and the time ashore between them is so short, that if the captain has a family or any pressing personal matters, he doesn't bother much with his ship in port but leaves everything to the owners until she's ready for sea. Still, it's always wise to have a look at him before irrevocably putting yourself in his hands. Turning back, I found Captain Peleg and asked where Captain Ahab might be.
"And what do you want with Captain Ahab? Everything's fine — you're signed on."
"Yes, but I'd like to see him."

"I don't think you'll be able to right now. I don't know exactly what's the matter with him, but he stays shut up inside his house. He's a sort of sick, and yet he doesn't look it. Actually, he isn't sick — but he isn't well either. Anyway, young man, he won't always see even me, so I don't suppose he'll see you. He's a strange man, Captain Ahab — so some think — but a good one. Oh, you'll like him well enough, no fear. He's a grand, ungodly, god-like man, Captain Ahab. He doesn't talk much, but when he does, you'd better listen. Be warned: Ahab is above the common run. He's been in colleges as well as among cannibals. He's faced deeper wonders than the waves and driven his fiery lance into mightier, stranger enemies than whales. His lance! The keenest and truest that ever came from all our island! Oh, he's not Captain Bildad, no, and he's not Captain Peleg. He's Ahab, boy. And Ahab of old, as you know, was a crowned king!"
"And a very wicked one. When that evil king was killed, the dogs licked his blood, did they not?"

"Come here — closer, closer," said Peleg, with a look in his eye that nearly startled me. "Listen, lad. Never say that aboard the Pequod. Never say it anywhere. Captain Ahab did not name himself. It was a foolish, ignorant whim of his crazy, widowed mother, who died when he was only a year old. And yet the old woman Tistig, at Gay Head, said the name would somehow prove prophetic. Other fools may tell you the same. I want to warn you — it's a lie. I know Captain Ahab well. I've sailed with him as mate, years ago. I know what he is — a good man. Not a pious, good man like Bildad, but a swearing good man — something like me — only there's a good deal more of him. I'll admit he was never very cheerful. And I know that on the way home last voyage, he was a little out of his mind for a while. But that was the sharp, shooting pains in his bleeding stump — anyone could see that. I know, too, that ever since he lost his leg on the last voyage to that accursed whale, he's been moody — desperately moody, and savage sometimes. But that will pass. And once and for all, let me tell you and assure you, young man: it's better to sail with a moody good captain than a laughing bad one. So goodbye — and don't wrong Captain Ahab just because he happens to have a wicked name. Besides, my boy, he has a wife — married not three voyages ago — a sweet, patient girl. Think about that. By that sweet girl, the old man has a child. Can you really believe there's any utter, hopeless evil in Ahab? No, no, my lad. Stricken and blasted as he may be, Ahab still has his humanity!"

As I walked away, I was full of thoughts. What had been revealed to me about Captain Ahab filled me with a strange, vague unease. Somehow, I felt both sympathy and sorrow for him, though I couldn't say why — unless it was the cruel loss of his leg. And yet I also felt a strange awe of him, though not exactly awe. I don't know what it was. But I felt it, and it didn't turn me against him, even though I was frustrated by what seemed like mystery surrounding him, as little as I knew of him then. Eventually, though, my thoughts turned in other directions, and for the time being, dark Ahab slipped from my mind.
